School Buildings

On June 26, 2025, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania filed criminal charges and a deferred prosecution agreement against the School District of Philadelphia — the first time in U.S. history a school district was criminally charged under AHERA, the federal asbestos-hazard statute. Eight criminal counts span June 2018 to April 2023; 61 findings document problems in 31 schools from 2015 to 2023; SDP must comply with monitoring and remediation requirements for five years for the charges to be dismissed. The state-constitutional context: the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court's February 2023 William Penn ruling (final July 2023) declared the state's school funding system unconstitutional under the Education Clause and equal protection grounds — Pennsylvania funds schools at a lower percentage from state sources than all but six other states, and the local-property-tax reliance maps local wealth onto educational opportunity. SDP's environmental management budget grew from $10.2 million in FY21 to $55.7 million in FY25 (a 5.5× increase) to meet AHERA enforcement; the District simultaneously faces a $300 million budget deficit, 85 buildings rated poor or unsatisfactory, 70,000 empty seats, and a proposed $3 billion 10-year Facilities Master Plan ("Accelerating Opportunity") with $2 billion requested from state and philanthropic sources. The structural finding: federal-criminal-floor enforcement (AHERA) operates simultaneously with state-constitutional inadequacy of funding (William Penn). SDP cannot use William Penn as a defense to AHERA non-compliance, but federal AHERA financing for compliance is essentially absent — the carry-forward structural mismatch most distinctive to this domain.

Legal Architecture

Constitutional foundation

The legal architecture governing school buildings rests on multiple constitutional foundations operating simultaneously, making this sub-domain unusually constitutionally dense.

PA Constitution Article III § 14 (Education Clause). "The General Assembly shall provide for the maintenance and support of a thorough and efficient system of public education to serve the needs of the Commonwealth." This is the foundation for the William Penn School District v. PDE ruling, which found Pennsylvania's school funding system unconstitutional. The constitutional violation is in the funding system — operating funding, capital funding, and the relationship between them — and is therefore directly material to school building capital analysis.

PA Equal Protection. The William Penn ruling also found violation of the state Constitution's equal protection provisions. The funding system creates structurally unequal opportunity by tying educational resources to local wealth. School building capital is one expression of this structural inequality: low-wealth districts cannot finance adequate facilities; high-wealth districts can.

14th Amendment Equal Protection (federal). Federal equal protection grounds for educational equity, particularly in the context of facility conditions and racial disparities. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. § 2000d) operationalizes this for federally-funded education programs.

PA Constitution Article I § 27 (Environmental Rights Amendment). Applies to school environmental quality — lead, asbestos, water quality, indoor air quality — to the extent that environmental quality of school facilities implicates the constitutional environmental rights of children educated in those facilities. Less developed in case law for schools specifically, but available as a doctrinal hook.

Federal Commerce Clause and Spending Clause. Federal authority over school environmental hazards (AHERA for asbestos; Title X for lead paint; SDWA for school drinking water) operates through these federal grounds. ESSA and McKinney-Vento operate under Spending Clause authority.

The constitutional tension specific to schools: William Penn establishes that Pennsylvania's funding system is constitutionally deficient, but the remedy is uncertain. The Court did not order a specific funding level; remedy implementation rests with the legislature. School capital is part of the constitutional violation but is also part of a system whose constitutional repair is incomplete. The AHERA criminal enforcement (June 2025 DPA) overlays this state-constitutional context with federal-criminal-floor enforcement: regardless of state funding architecture's constitutional adequacy, federal AHERA requirements operate as a federal floor that the SDP must meet.

Federal architecture

AHERA — Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act, 15 U.S.C. § 2641 et seq. — Title II of the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA). Enacted in 1986 to require public schools to meet monitoring and remediation requirements to reduce exposure to damaged asbestos by students, teachers, and others. School districts are required every three years to conduct detailed inspections of their buildings and remediate damaged asbestos and every six months to conduct less intensive visual inspections to ensure areas containing asbestos remain safe. EPA implementing regulations at 40 CFR Part 763.

AHERA enforcement against the School District of Philadelphia. On June 26, 2025, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania filed criminal charges and a deferred prosecution agreement against the School District of Philadelphia. U.S. Attorney David Metcalf announced the charges and DPA. This was the first time in U.S. history that a school district was criminally charged with this type of environmental violation, and the first use of a DPA in a case against a public school district in an AHERA case. The charges are the result of a five-year investigation conducted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, the Department of Justice Environmental Crimes Section, and the Environmental Protection Agency's Criminal Investigations Division (EPA-CID).

The DPA includes:

  • Eight criminal counts between June 2018 and April 2023 involving failures to conduct mandatory three-year inspections at at least seven schools (S. Weir Mitchell Elementary, Charles W. Henry Elementary, and others), plus failure to conduct a timely six-month inspection at one school (Building 21 Alternative High School).
  • 61 findings in the DPA, citing problems in 31 schools from 2015 to 2023, including improperly covered asbestos with duct tape, shuttered buildings, and unsafe remediation efforts.
  • Five-year monitoring period. If a court finds the District meets its inspection and remediation requirements for five years, the criminal charges will be dropped.
  • Regular compliance reports to the federal court for five years.

The AHERA enforcement context is critical because it represents an active federal-criminal-floor enforcement mechanism operating simultaneously with the state-constitutional inadequacy of funding. The SDP cannot use William Penn as a defense to AHERA non-compliance: federal floor obligations are not contingent on state funding adequacy.

Federal funding for school facilities. Direct federal funding for school construction is limited. The principal federal pathway is through CDBG (HUD) for "public facilities and improvements," but CDBG is not generally usable for school buildings (with limited exceptions). The Supporting America's School Infrastructure (SASI) Grant Program provides federal technical assistance funding to PDE; the Pennsylvania Department of Education was recently awarded a SASI Grant to increase capacity to support high-need districts and schools in leveraging other available federal, state, and local resources to improve school facilities and environments.

The IIJA provided some school-relevant funding through cross-cutting programs (e.g., school bus electrification under EPA Clean School Bus Program) but did not include a major school capital authority. Federal IRA (Inflation Reduction Act) provisions affecting public-building energy efficiency may have provided indirect support for school energy upgrades; however, OBBBA (P.L. 119-21, July 4, 2025) repealed or rescinded significant portions of IRA infrastructure-relevant funding, including the $100M for state and local environmental review capacity-building, and phased out clean-vehicle and EV-charging infrastructure tax credits by mid-2026 — affecting the federal funding context for school energy and electric school bus initiatives going forward.

Federal funding flow. Federal direct school funding is primarily operational (Title I, ESSA programs, IDEA special education, school nutrition), not capital. The principal federal capital pathway for SDP would be IIJA-related programs (Clean School Bus; energy efficiency) plus AHERA-related compliance funds (which require district expenditure but are not federal grants — federal funding for AHERA compliance is essentially nil; SDP must finance compliance from district resources).

State architecture

Public School Code of 1949, 24 P.S. § 1-101 et seq. — the comprehensive Pennsylvania statute governing public education, including capital reimbursement provisions in Articles 7 and 25. Specific PlanCon provisions: 24 P.S. § 7-733 (Basic Education Circular reference), 24 P.S. § 25-2574 (Reimbursements for School Construction Bond Issues), 24 P.S. § 25-2575, 24 P.S. § 25-2578 (PlanCon-related). Implementing regulations at 22 Pa. Code § 349.20 et seq.

William Penn School District v. PDE et al. Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court Judge Renée Cohn Jubelirer issued the decision on February 7, 2023. The 786-page decision declared Pennsylvania's school funding system unconstitutional under both the Education Clause and equal protection provisions. The Court held that "education is a fundamental right under Pennsylvania's constitution" — the first explicit Pennsylvania holding to that effect. Republican legislative leaders filed a motion for post-trial relief on February 17, 2023; that motion was denied. The July 21, 2023 deadline for filing an appeal to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court passed without action — the ruling became final on that date.

Adequacy gap findings and legislative response. Per the Education Law Center analysis cited in the William Penn proceedings, Pennsylvania schools were initially underfunded by approximately $4.6 billion to $6.2 billion. Per the Education Law Center December 2025 update: in the 2024–25 and 2025–26 budgets, the legislature has invested approximately $1 billion toward closing the unconstitutional funding gap, leaving a remaining adequacy gap of approximately $3.8 billion.

Pennsylvania state FY 2025–26 budget enactment. The Pennsylvania state FY 2025–26 budget was enacted on November 12, 2025 — Day 135 of an unprecedented budget impasse, the longest in state history. The enacted budget allocated $565 million in adequacy-related school funding: approximately $526.4 million through the bipartisan adequacy formula, $32.2 million in tax equity supplement, and $6.4 million through a minimum-baseline provision guaranteeing each of approximately 500 districts at least $50,000 in additional funding. The William Penn School District received approximately $80 million in total combined funding under the FY 2025–26 budget. The budget also included $665 million for total public schools, $175 million in cyber charter reform, and $125 million for school facilities — though the facility allocation is not formally tied to the William Penn formula and does not address school capital adequacy through the constitutional remedy structure.

Governor Shapiro's FY 2026–27 budget proposal (February 19, 2026). Proposes an additional $565 million for school districts with adequacy gap. As of April 27, 2026, the FY 2026–27 budget has not been enacted; the deadline is June 30, 2026.

The post-William Penn capital landscape. The decision applies to the entire school funding system; capital is an integral component. However, the legislative response has primarily addressed operating funding gaps. PlanCon — the historical Pennsylvania school construction reimbursement program — has been in moratorium since 2015–16: 2012 — legislature began limiting PlanCon applications. 2015–16 — state stopped funding PlanCon, zeroing out a budget line that had reached more than $300 million annually. 2019 — Act 70 of 2019 reauthorized PlanCon as PlanCon 2.0 with streamlined approval process; legislature never authorized funding. Ongoing — PDE continues administering approximately 2,800 bonds for approximately 430 districts and AVTSes from pre-moratorium projects, at approximately $235 million annual cost. PlanCon 2.0 is currently NOT accepting applications. 2023–24 budget — $100 million for a PlanCon-style program plus $75 million for unsafe facilities (50% match, $10M maximum grant). 2024–25 budget request from Governor Shapiro — $300 million for the Public School Facility Improvement Grant Program and $50 million for the Public School Environmental Repairs Grant Program.

Pennsylvania Department of Education (PDE). State-level education authority. PDE Bureau of Budget and Fiscal Management administers PlanCon reimbursement (for pre-moratorium projects) and the new PA Public School Facility Improvement Grant Program. Division of School Facilities oversees Act 34 compliance.

Pennsylvania-specific features. Pennsylvania funds schools at a lower percentage from state sources than most other states. Per William Penn proceedings: Pennsylvania is more reliant on local property taxpayers to fund schools than all but six other states, with only 38 percent of funding coming from the state level. This local-property-tax reliance is the structural mechanism through which local wealth maps onto educational opportunity — and is the constitutional violation William Penn identified.

Local architecture

School District of Philadelphia (SDP). Independent school district under Pennsylvania Public School Code. Returned to local control in 2018 after twenty years of state takeover (1998–2018, including the School Reform Commission era). Currently enrolls approximately 114,000 students (down from a historical peak of approximately 200,000). Operates approximately 200 active buildings (or 300+ depending on inclusion of closed/leased properties).

Superintendent: Tony B. Watlington Sr., since June 2022. Board of Education President: Reginald Streater.

Facilities Master Plan ("Accelerating Opportunity"). SDP is finalizing its 10-year facilities plan. Plan evolution:

  • January 22, 2026: SDP released the initial set of recommendations.
  • February 26, 2026: Superintendent Watlington presented the first version of "Accelerating Opportunity" to the Board of Education.
  • April 20, 2026: Watlington presented the second and final version to the Board.
  • April 23, 2026: Board meeting; vote postponed.
  • April 30, 2026: rescheduled vote (pending as of this analysis — outcome unknown).

Final plan parameters (as presented April 20, 2026): 17 school closures beginning in school year 2027–28 (revised down from 20 in the January version); 169 schools modernized (revised up from 159 in the January version); six school co-locations (maintained through revisions); $3 billion total cost (revised up from $2.8 billion in the January version). The District plans to put $1 billion towards the upgrades and is requesting $2 billion from state and philanthropic sources. The Board of Education vote was originally scheduled for April 23, 2026 but was delayed to April 30, 2026 "in the spirit of partnership with the communities we serve" (per Board President Streater) at City Council request.

SDP fiscal context. $300 million budget deficit — stems primarily from the expiration of federal pandemic relief dollars. 85 buildings in poor or unsatisfactory condition. 70,000 empty seats across the district. $225 million in budget cuts proposed for next school year, eliminating 220 building substitute positions and reassigning 340 school-based roles. Mayor Parker $1 rideshare tax proposal would generate approximately $48–54 million annually if approved; would go into effect January 1, 2027. Uber launched a six-figure advertising campaign opposing the tax. District maintenance backlog: approximately $7 billion (per PFT President Arthur Steinberg, 2024 — large-scale estimate including facilities that would be cheaper to replace than repair).

SDP environmental management response (post-investigation). In response to the AHERA investigation, SDP's environmental management budget grew from $10.2 million in Fiscal Year 2021 to $55.7 million in Fiscal Year 2025 — a 5.5× increase over four years. Eighteen new positions were added to the Office of Environmental Management and Services. SDP entered a $24.2 million multi-year contract with Tetra Tech, a consulting and engineering firm, to ramp up inspections. SDP "tripled our investment in environmental management with support from the University of Pennsylvania" (per Superintendent Watlington's June 2025 statement) — Penn's $100 million donation was pledged the same year as the federal probe began (2020), though the specific operational support arrangement is not fully documented in available sources. All District-owned schools are now inspected twice per year, per the District; all inspection reports are publicly posted on the SDP website.

Frankford High School (PA-3) closed in 2023 due to extensive damaged asbestos. Plans to spend approximately $20 million to fix the school could lead to reopening for the 2025–26 school year. Students of Frankford High are either attending school in an annexed building or at Roberto Clemente Middle School in North Philadelphia.

Philadelphia City Council interaction. Council Education Committee Chair Isaiah Thomas and Council Majority Leader Katherine Gilmore Richardson are the central legislative interlocutors with SDP. Tensions between Council and SDP over the facilities plan (April 2026) center on perceived inadequate community notice, scope of closures, and whether the rideshare tax proposal can be advanced if closures proceed.

Philadelphia / SDP fiscal relationship. Per the Finance & Taxation handoff: the fiscal gap between anchor institution tax-exempt property footprint (approximately $100–200M annually, structural estimate) and PILOET receipts (approximately $10–30M annually) means the School District bears approximately $25–60M annually in net foregone revenue. SDP's capital constraint is a function of operating constraint, which is partly a function of the city's PILOET fiscal architecture, which is partly a function of anchor institution tax-exempt property holdings.

Federal funding flow at the local level. SDP is an LEA (Local Educational Agency) receiving federal Title I, IDEA, and other operating funds directly from PDE pass-through and from USED. Capital funding from federal sources is minimal. AHERA compliance funding is district-financed; AHERA enforcement provides federal monitoring overlay without federal financial assistance. The Penn arrangement provides anchor institution support outside the federal-funding architecture.

Home Rule authority and limits. Philadelphia has limited authority over SDP fiscal decisions. SDP is an independent school district; Philadelphia provides some general fund contribution but does not directly govern SDP. Closure decisions go through state hearings under Pennsylvania Public School Code. The City's leverage on SDP is exercised through Council appropriations, mayoral coordination, and state-level advocacy — not through direct authority.

Geography & representation

Data provenance. SDP October 1, 2024 Enrollment Snapshot; SDP Office of Environmental Management and Services public inspection reports; PWD's lead-pipe inventory work intersecting with school water testing; the November 12, 2025 enacted PA FY 2025–26 budget; Education Law Center December 2025 William Penn analysis; the June 26, 2025 USAO-EDPA criminal information and DPA; SDP Board of Education materials for the Facilities Master Plan ("Accelerating Opportunity"); Philadelphia City Council Education Committee proceedings; Inquirer, Chalkbeat, and WHYY education reporting.

Enrollment. Per SDP's October 1, 2024 Enrollment Snapshot, total Philadelphia public school enrollment was 198,299 students. Of those, 117,956 were enrolled in District and Alternative schools (114,529 in District schools, 3,427 in Alternative); 63,964 were enrolled in Philadelphia Charter schools; and 12,852 were enrolled in Cyber Charter schools. Public school enrollment in the city is 1.9 times greater than charter school enrollment and 3.9 times that of private school enrollment. Approximately 70% of school-age children attended public schools (2018 baseline), 22.7% private, and 7.3% reported as not enrolled. As of 2018, approximately 283,991 Philadelphians were between the ages of 5 and 19 — about 18% of the city's total population — though that share has been in decline.

Among District students in 2024–25, Spanish was the most common non-English language spoken at home; Portuguese had risen rapidly to surpass Mandarin Chinese as the second most common non-English home language. The District's racial and ethnic composition reflects the historical and present demographic geography of Philadelphia: Black students are the only racial or ethnic group with a higher enrollment concentration in the city's charter schools than in District schools (per Economy League analysis of 2019–2020 data).

Building inventory and condition. Per the "Accelerating Opportunity" Facilities Master Plan, SDP operates approximately 200 active school buildings (with additional closed/leased properties bringing the total higher). 85 buildings are in poor or unsatisfactory condition. The District has approximately 70,000 empty seats across the system. Total cost of the proposed 10-year facilities plan is $3 billion; the District plans to put $1 billion toward upgrades and is requesting $2 billion from state and philanthropic sources. The Mayor Parker $1 rideshare tax proposal would generate approximately $48–54 million annually if approved (effective January 1, 2027). The District faces a $300 million budget deficit, with $225 million in budget cuts proposed for next school year — eliminating 220 building substitute positions and reassigning 340 school-based roles.

AHERA enforcement context. The June 26, 2025 DPA filed by USAO-EDPA against SDP includes 8 criminal counts naming 7 schools (including S. Weir Mitchell Elementary and Charles W. Henry Elementary), 61 findings citing problems in 31 schools from 2015–2023, a 5-year monitoring period, and dismissal upon compliance. SDP's environmental management budget grew from $10.2 million in FY21 to $55.7 million in FY25. Eighteen positions added to the Office of Environmental Management and Services. SDP entered a $24.2 million multi-year contract with Tetra Tech for inspections. Penn donated $100 million to support environmental management (pledged 2020). Frankford High School (PA-3) closed in 2023 due to extensive damaged asbestos with plans to spend approximately $20 million to fix the school for potential 2025–26 reopening.

William Penn fiscal context. The February 7, 2023 William Penn School District v. PDE ruling (Judge Cohn Jubelirer; 786-page; final July 21, 2023) declared Pennsylvania's school funding system unconstitutional under both Education Clause and equal protection grounds. Per Education Law Center analysis: $4.6–6.2B initial adequacy gap; approximately $1B invested across 2024–25 and 2025–26 budgets; approximately $3.8B remaining adequacy gap. The November 12, 2025 enacted PA FY 2025–26 budget allocated $565M toward the adequacy formula ($526.4M adequacy + $32.2M tax equity + $6.4M minimum-baseline). Pennsylvania is more reliant on local property taxpayers to fund schools than all but six other states, with only 38 percent of funding coming from the state level.

Geographic variation across four sub-areas.

  • North/Northwest Philadelphia Core. Substantial SDP enrollment in catchment elementary, middle, and high schools serving lower-income, predominantly Black and Latino neighborhoods. Schools include Frankford High School (closed 2023, asbestos), and a number of catchment schools serving North Philadelphia. Building condition concentrations in the 85 "poor or unsatisfactory" inventory tend to be higher in older, deferred-maintenance buildings disproportionately located in this sub-area. The seven schools named in the 8-count DPA span multiple sub-areas. The William Penn ruling's finding of structural underfunding tied to local property taxpayer reliance has differential consequences for this sub-area: with lower local property tax base relative to higher-wealth Pennsylvania districts, North/Northwest Core schools depend disproportionately on the state share of education funding — and the structural underfunding diagnosed by William Penn is therefore differentially consequential here.
  • West Philadelphia Core. Catchment schools serving West Philadelphia neighborhoods including Cobbs Creek, Walnut Hill, Cedar Park, Mantua, Powelton, Mill Creek, and adjacent areas. Anchor institution proximity (Penn, Drexel) creates a complex educational geography: Penn-affiliated programs and university-school-partnership models operate in this sub-area, and Penn's $100M donation pledged in 2020 anchors part of the increased SDP environmental management capacity. Penn Alexander School (a Penn-funded catchment public school) is in this sub-area. The structural feature: anchor institutions are tax-exempt for property tax purposes, creating the PILOET fiscal architecture in which the city forgoes property tax revenue from the institutions that generate substantial economic activity.
  • Northwest Philadelphia. SDP schools serving Manayunk, Roxborough, East Falls, Germantown, Mt. Airy, and Chestnut Hill neighborhoods. Charles W. Henry Elementary (named in AHERA DPA) is in Mt. Airy. Building age varies in this sub-area: the Northwest contains some of Philadelphia's older school buildings (concentrated in Germantown and Mt. Airy historic districts) and some newer construction. School-age population density is generally lower than in the Cores; per-school enrollment patterns differ. Some Northwest schools have produced strong School Progress Report scores; others face the same building-condition challenges as schools in the Cores.
  • South/Southwest Philadelphia. SDP schools serving South Philadelphia (Point Breeze, Grays Ferry, etc.) and Southwest Philadelphia (Eastwick, Kingsessing, Elmwood, etc.). South Philadelphia High School and other large catchment schools are in this sub-area. The Lower Darby Creek Superfund Site adjacency in Eastwick raises environmental quality questions for any schools in close proximity (cross-reference to the Solid Waste & Sanitation environmental-justice analysis).

The geographic variation pattern in this sub-domain is structurally complex because the unit of analysis is the school building, and school buildings span sub-areas in ways that don't map cleanly to the four-sub-area framework. The 17 proposed closures in the Facilities Master Plan, the 169 modernizations, and the 6 co-locations are distributed across all four sub-areas, with concentration patterns reflecting the underlying building-condition distribution.

Representation question. PA Constitution Article III § 14 (Education Clause) guarantees a "thorough and efficient" system of public education. PA equal protection grounds the William Penn ruling's finding of unconstitutional disparity. 14th Amendment federal equal protection grounds Title VI as applied to federally-funded education programs. PA Article I § 27 provides substantive constitutional review for environmental conditions in schools. Federal AHERA (15 U.S.C. § 2641 et seq.) provides criminal-floor enforcement for asbestos hazards. Federal SDWA applies to school drinking water. Federal Title I, IDEA, and ESSA programs provide operating support. State PA Public School Code establishes the comprehensive state framework; PlanCon was the historical capital reimbursement program (in moratorium since 2015–16; PlanCon 2.0 authorized 2019 but unfunded). Local SDP independent school district governance (returned to local control 2018); Board of Education and Superintendent Watlington administration.

What PA-3 students and families experience is SDP school buildings through 85 buildings rated poor or unsatisfactory, 70,000 empty seats indicating excess capacity, AHERA-cited deficiencies in 31 schools across 2015–2023, the closure of Frankford High due to asbestos, and the proposed closure of 17 schools in the Facilities Master Plan with associated community concerns. The William Penn structural underfunding diagnosis means that resources for building condition, educational programming, and operating capacity are below the level the Pennsylvania Constitution requires — a state-constitutional finding with direct material consequences for PA-3 students.

The mismatch between formal provision and actual experience is structural and constitutionally diagnosed. The William Penn ruling identified the local-property-tax-reliance structural feature as the constitutional violation: tying educational resources to local wealth produces inadequate funding for districts with lower local property tax base, including SDP. The structural underfunding has cumulative consequences across operating funding, capital funding, environmental compliance funding, and facility maintenance funding. AHERA enforcement is federal-criminal-floor and cannot be defended against by citing state funding inadequacy — the federal floor requires compliance regardless of state funding architecture. The structural result is a configuration in which SDP must comply with federal AHERA requirements while the underlying funding architecture is constitutionally inadequate. The Mayor Parker $1 rideshare tax proposal, the Penn anchor institution support, the philanthropic component of the $2B requested ask, and the Public School Facility Improvement Grant Program represent partial responses; the November 2025 enacted $565M PA budget allocation toward William Penn adequacy is incremental progress but does not resolve the constitutional underfunding diagnosis (approximately $3.8B remaining adequacy gap).

Federal House representation for PA-3 has direct levers on the federal portions of this sub-domain: AHERA enforcement engagement with DOJ and EPA Region III; federal funding advocacy through IIJA cross-cutting provisions, IRA energy-efficiency provisions, and any future federal school capital programs; SDWA enforcement attention for school drinking water; Title VI cumulative-impact analysis for the geographic distribution of building-condition concentration. Federal representation has indirect levers on state-level structures through congressional delegation coordination, federal-funding conditions, and federal-state-collaborative programs. The William Penn ruling is a state-constitutional finding; federal House representation does not have direct authority over the state remedy, but federal-program advocacy, federal-funding flow that affects state fiscal capacity, and inter-jurisdictional coordination are levers federal representation can use. The most consequential federal-floor question for this sub-domain may be the gap between AHERA's enforcement scope and the federal-funding architecture's silence on AHERA compliance financing — a gap that, if addressed, would link federal-criminal-floor environmental enforcement to federal financial assistance for compliance.

Gap analysis

Gap 1 — AHERA federal compliance financing absence. Federal AHERA enforcement (15 U.S.C. § 2641 et seq.) operates as a federal-criminal-floor obligation; the June 26, 2025 DPA against SDP demonstrates active enforcement, with the District operating under judicial oversight as of December 2025 reporting. Federal financial assistance to support AHERA compliance is essentially absent — SDP must finance compliance ($55.7M FY25 environmental management budget; $24.2M Tetra Tech contract) from district resources. The structural gap between federal-criminal-floor enforcement scope and federal-funding architecture's silence on AHERA compliance financing is the most distinctive federal-floor gap in the physical-infrastructure domain. Federal House representation can advocate for federal AHERA compliance financing as new program development; this is the most actionable federal-floor gap surfaced in the domain.

Gap 2 — William Penn $3.8B remaining adequacy gap notwithstanding partial legislative response. The William Penn ruling (final July 21, 2023) declared Pennsylvania's school funding system constitutionally inadequate. Per Education Law Center December 2025 analysis: $4.6–6.2B initial adequacy gap; approximately $1B invested across 2024–25 and 2025–26 budgets; approximately $3.8B remaining gap. The November 12, 2025 enacted PA FY 2025–26 budget allocated $565M ($526.4M adequacy + $32.2M tax equity + $6.4M minimum-baseline); William Penn School District itself received approximately $80M total. Governor Shapiro's FY 2026–27 budget proposal (February 2026) includes an additional proposed $565M but is not yet enacted as of April 2026. The state-constitutional inadequacy applies to the whole funding system including capital and operations; SDP capital constraints (Facilities Master Plan $3B with $2B requested from state and philanthropic sources) are partly a function of operating constraint. Not directly federal — state-constitutional remedy rests with PA legislature. Federal House representation has indirect levers through federal-funding flow that affects state fiscal capacity and through advocacy with state delegation.

Gap 3 — PlanCon 2.0 unfunded since 2019. Act 70 of 2019 reauthorized the Pennsylvania school construction reimbursement program as PlanCon 2.0 with streamlined approval process; the legislature has not authorized funding for PlanCon 2.0. Existing program administers approximately 2,800 pre-moratorium bonds for approximately 430 districts at approximately $235M annual cost. Governor Shapiro's 2024–25 budget request ($300M Public School Facility Improvement Grant Program + $50M Public School Environmental Repairs Grant Program) and the 2023–24 budget allocation ($100M PlanCon-style + $75M unsafe facilities) represent partial responses. The November 2025 enacted FY 2025–26 budget included $125M for school facilities — though the facility allocation is not formally tied to the William Penn formula and does not address school capital adequacy through the constitutional remedy structure. Not directly federal. Federal House representation can advocate for federal IIJA-cross-cutting school capital funding (limited under current architecture) and for any future federal school-capital program development.

Gap 4 — Title VI cumulative-impact analysis for building condition concentration. 85 SDP buildings are rated poor or unsatisfactory; condition concentration in older buildings disproportionately located in the Cores; AHERA findings distributed across 31 schools 2015–2023 and 7 schools named in DPA criminal counts. Federal Title VI cumulative-impact analysis for the geographic distribution of building-condition concentration is structurally analogous to the HIN cumulative-impact gap in the roads sub-domain — formal Title VI review at project level produces uneven coverage of the cumulative pattern. The post-2025 retraction of EO 14008, EO 12898, and EO 14096, alongside closure of EPA's regional EJ offices, has thinned the federal administrative architecture for cumulative-impact review without changing the underlying Title VI statutory floor. Federal House representation can advocate for cumulative-impact Title VI analysis with USED, EPA, and DOJ.

Gap 5 — Anchor institution / SDP environmental management support transparency. SDP's environmental management capacity grew from $10.2M FY21 to $55.7M FY25, with Superintendent Watlington's June 2025 statement attributing some of the support to the University of Pennsylvania's $100M donation pledged in 2020 (the year the federal probe began). The specific operational mechanism by which Penn's $100M flows to SDP environmental management is not fully documented in available public sources. Not directly federal but cross-references the Finance & Taxation PILOET fiscal architecture (anchor institution tax-exempt status) and could intersect with federal anchor-institution-related programs.

Gap 6 — Federal IIJA cross-cutting school capital programs limited; OBBBA further narrowed federal program horizon. Federal IIJA included some school-relevant funding through cross-cutting programs (Clean School Bus Program; energy-efficiency adjacencies) but did not include a major school capital authority. The Supporting America's School Infrastructure (SASI) Grant Program provides federal technical assistance to PDE but operates at limited scale. Following the July 4, 2025 enactment of OBBBA (P.L. 119-21), the federal environmental review capacity-building program ($100M IRA appropriation) was repealed, and clean-vehicle and EV-charging tax credits were phased out — narrowing the federal program horizon for school energy and electric school bus initiatives in addition to broader IRA program rescissions. Federal advocacy for school capital program development; engagement with surviving IRA energy-efficiency program implementation; reauthorization advocacy for IIJA cross-cutting program protection.
